title: What People Don’t Know About Siegfried Engelmann and Direct Instruction
author: Linda Diamond
summary: Linda Diamond, a former teacher and executive director of the Evidence Advocacy Center, responds to the reaction to Emily Hanford's Sold a Story season two, which centres on Siegfried Engelmann's Direct Instruction. An editor's note from Robert Pondiscio introduces her essay. She takes on two misconceptions: that scripted lessons strip teachers of creativity and that DI is only useful for decoding. Drawing on her use of Decoding and Comprehension materials with struggling high school readers in the 1970s, she says the scripts freed her to focus on students and that the class went on to read Cyrano de Bergerac. She argues critics confuse what is taught with how it is taught, noting that later programs such as Reading Mastery Signature, the Language series, and Reasoning and Writing build vocabulary, background knowledge, oral language, and logical reasoning. Her conclusion is that Engelmann rejected false dichotomies between skills and knowledge.
points: Diamond rebuts the charge that scripts remove creativity by recalling that the scripts freed her to focus on students, in her words she was still the conductor.
She distinguishes content from pedagogy: explicit, clear instruction can teach rich domain knowledge as well as decoding.
Critics may be judging DI by an early decoding-focused edition, whereas later editions include unabridged literary texts and informational background.
Programs like Language for Learning and Reasoning and Writing show DI addressing oral language and logical thinking, areas she says are widely neglected.
The broader lesson is to avoid false dichotomies between skill building and knowledge, a point that bears on current science of reading debates.
quotes: Direct Instruction is a tightly structured, highly interactive, teacher-led instructional design model developed in the 1960s by Zig Engelmann and his colleagues. It rests on the idea that “If the learner hasn’t learned, the teacher hasn’t taught.

Much of the negative reaction is based on a snapshot of Reading Mastery Classic, Zig’s PK–3 reading program, which does not reflect the entire corpus of Zig’s work. Others simply appear to be ignorant about what DI is.

The scripts freed me from writing lesson plans from scratch, allowed me to focus on the students, and ultimately supercharged my instruction. The scripts also taught me how to actively engage my students rather than simply state information to them.

This is the story that I tell people when they object that DI’s scripted lessons take the joy or creativity out of classrooms. I also tell them that DI may have given me the precise music notes in the precise order, but I was still the conductor.

This misconception confuses what content is taught with how it is taught, the pedagogy. Explicit and clear pedagogy is not reserved only for decoding; it also is applicable to teaching rich, challenging, domain-specific knowledge.
Oral language development is a widely neglected component of literacy; we are only recently beginning to hear about it even from fervent science of reading advocates.
Zig never accepted false dichotomies, and neither should we. He never wanted students who decoded without knowledge, nor did he believe explicit skill building excluded rich content.
